Recent work supports separating semantic relatedness from user preference. *Disentangling Likes and Dislikes* (2024/WWW 2025) finds that strong textual-similarity scores do not ensure explanations reflect users’ positive or negative opinions; its review-based supervision is unavailable here, so only its evaluation distinction transfers. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13248). *Beyond Explicit and Implicit* (2025), based on interviews with 34 users, distinguishes feedback intentions from observable consumption behavior—supporting caution when interpreting interactions as immediate desire or rejection. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09869).

Suggested diagnostic protocol, synthesized from these findings: annotate explicit immediate choice, broad relatedness, explicit rejection, and insufficient evidence separately; record redundancy as an additional flag. Require supporting feedback excerpts or history/item references, document temporal scope, and leave ownership, compatibility and mood unknown unless stated. Independently double-code a sample; report raw agreement, nominal Krippendorff’s alpha, label counts and adjudicated disagreements. The 2025 HCI+NLP proceedings recommend recording evidence/reasoning to support disagreement review and discuss agreement measures. [Proceedings](https://aclanthology.org/2025.hcinlp-1.pdf).

For automated annotation, *Trust or Escalate* (ICLR 2025) calibrates judge-confidence thresholds against human labels to control disagreement while retaining coverage. [Paper](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/08dabd5345b37fffcbe335bd578b15a0-Paper-Conference.pdf). Adaptation: calibrate on separate human annotations; report coverage, error among accepted judgments and risk–coverage curves. Keep insufficient evidence as a substantive label, distinct from evaluator abstention. These diagnostic judgments supplement the fixed macro validation HR@10 selection metric; they do not establish purchase intent or future utility.
